design_detail: Literature review with a systematic search and descriptive synthesis, no meta-analysis (J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2017;88(12):1079–1091; review article, free). EMBASE, MEDLINE and PsycINFO searched to 10 February 2017, plus reference lists; English or a detailed English abstract; no year limit. 370 records screened, 77 papers included: 3 post-mortem series (Table 2), 11 case-control, cohort and case-series studies (Table 3) and 63 case reports and series describing 98 strokes in people aged 44 or younger (Table 1: 81 haemorrhagic, 17 ischaemic). Cases were pooled by counting; no protocol, risk-of-bias assessment or causality assessment of the case attributions. Methamphetamine and other amphetamines were both eligible (non-medical use only).
can_establish: What kinds of stroke have been reported in young people after non-medical methamphetamine or amphetamine use, with what imaging findings and reported outcomes, and which epidemiological studies had examined the association by early 2017.
cannot_establish: How often stroke occurs in people who use methamphetamine, the relative share of haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke, or case fatality, because 63 of the 77 sources are case reports selected by publication, about half the cases involved amphetamine rather than methamphetamine, deaths ascertained at autopsy are pooled with clinical cases, and the epidemiological estimates are reported without intervals or adjustment details.

sample.recruitment: Bibliographic search (EMBASE, MEDLINE, PsycINFO) to 10 February 2017 with hand-searching of reference lists (Methods). Cases in Table 1 date from 1945 to 2016 and come from clinical reports, coroner and forensic reports and three autopsy series. Table 3 studies come from US, Australian and Taiwanese hospital series, a US population-based database of hospitalized stroke (Westover et al. 2007), a case-control study of women (Petitti et al. 1998) and a Taiwanese cohort of 1315 people who used methamphetamine (Huang et al. 2016).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed publications (or ones referenced in a relevant journal article) on methamphetamine use and incident stroke, reporting cases aged 44 or younger; ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke; non-medical use only, excluding prescribed amphetamines (dextroamphetamine only when used non-medically). Polydrug use was recorded where reported (Methods › Inclusion criteria).
sample.demographics: Case reports (Table 1): ages 16 to 44. Haemorrhagic: 51 men and 30 women by the editors' count (text: 2:1); ischaemic: 12 men and 5 women. Editors' count from Table 1: 46 of the 98 cases list amphetamine, dextroamphetamine or amphetamine with ecstasy and do not name methamphetamine (43 of 81 haemorrhagic, 3 of 17 ischaemic).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Figure 1 (flow diagram) is an image and was not extracted; the abstract gives 370 screened and 77 included.
sample.selection_effects: Case reports are published when they are striking, severe or unusual; the authors acknowledge that this may explain the 80% haemorrhagic share and the poor outcomes. Ten of the 81 haemorrhagic cases come from autopsy series (Table 1 footnote †) and other deaths from coroner and forensic reports, so case fatality is inflated by design. English-language restriction. Attribution of each stroke to the drug rests on the original case authors; several cases had other causes or risk factors (syphilis, carotid dissection, bacterial embolus, arteriovenous malformation, aneurysm, hypertension, pregnancy-induced hypertension, smoking, oral contraceptive use) or long intervals since last use (2 weeks, 4 days, 3 months).

exposure.measurement: Not described at review level: the review does not say whether use in each case was established by toxicology, self-report or records. The drug column of Table 1 records what the case report named.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized for dose. Route is reported only as ratios: haemorrhagic oral:injection:inhalation 3:3:1; ischaemic 1:1:4 (Results). Table 1 has no route column and the number of cases with a known route is not stated. Time from use to symptoms ranged from minutes to weeks; in Table 1 one ischaemic stroke occurred 3 months after reported last use.
exposure.polysubstance: Recorded but not analysed. Editors' count from Table 1: 17 of 98 cases list another drug (heroin, cocaine, ecstasy or MDMA, cannabis, methylphenidate or caffeine): 15 haemorrhagic, 2 ischaemic. The Westover estimate is compared with cocaine and tobacco in the source study, but the review does not say what it was adjusted for.

comparison.controls: None for the case reports. Table 2: one post-mortem series compared 413 methamphetamine-positive deaths with 114 drug-free trauma deaths (Karch et al. 1999). Table 3: Petitti et al. (1021 controls), Westover et al. (hospitalized stroke patients by drug-use coding), Huang et al. (a control group, not described), Beadell et al. (age-matched controls).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: For the case reports, pre-existing vascular malformations, aneurysms and hypertension could be identified only where investigated; the authors note that many reports did not record other risk factors and that unreported risk factors cannot be excluded (Discussion › Individual and use-related characteristics).

outcomes.instruments: Stroke type, site, angiographic or autopsy findings and clinical outcome as recorded in each case report (Table 1); proportions, odds ratios, hazard ratios and Glasgow Outcome Scale results as reported by the primary studies (Tables 2 and 3).
outcomes.operationalization: Stroke in a person aged 44 or younger in whom the case authors linked the event to non-medical amphetamine-type stimulant use. Outcomes were classified by the reviewers as death, complete recovery or residual deficit from the case descriptions; criteria for complete recovery are not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates; counts and proportions only. Second-hand estimates, all without confidence intervals: Westover et al. (ages 18–44, 937 haemorrhagic and 998 ischaemic hospitalized strokes) OR 4.95 for haemorrhagic and 1.04 for ischaemic stroke with amphetamine use; Petitti et al. (women aged 15–44) 3.8 times the risk of stroke with amphetamine use; Kaku & Lowenstein (ages 15–44) relative risk of stroke with any illicit drug use 6.5 (ischaemic) and 11.7 (haemorrhagic) at age 35 or below; Huang et al. (1315 people who used methamphetamine, all ages, 54 stroke events) HR 2.09 (p=0.001) for haemorrhagic stroke, no significant difference for ischaemic stroke or subarachnoid haemorrhage. Amphetamines were implicated in 6–13% of haemorrhagic and 2–6% of ischaemic strokes in hospital series, and intracranial haemorrhage caused 1.4–5% of methamphetamine-related deaths in post-mortem series. Editors' calculation from Table 2: Karch et al.'s 10 of 413 (2.4%) versus 0 of 114 trauma controls gives a two-sided Fisher exact p of about 0.13, so these counts alone do not show the strong association attributed to that study.
analysis.covariates: Not reported for any second-hand estimate.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration mentioned. The search strategy is in online supplementary figure s1 (PDF, not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be fully assessed. The excluded-studies list and search strategy are in supplements (not read). Outcome proportions in the abstract are given only for the case reports, not for the epidemiological studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: 98 published cases of stroke in people aged 16–44 after non-medical use of methamphetamine or amphetamine (about half amphetamine), 83% haemorrhagic, with a third of haemorrhagic cases fatal in a pool that includes 10 autopsy-series deaths; three post-mortem series attributing 1.4–5% of methamphetamine-related deaths to intracranial haemorrhage; and a small epidemiological literature in which amphetamine use was associated with haemorrhagic stroke (Westover OR 4.95; Huang HR 2.09) but not with ischaemic stroke (Westover OR 1.04; Huang not significant).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions speak of methamphetamine throughout, while about half of the pooled cases involved amphetamine without methamphetamine. The conclusion that there is a preponderance of haemorrhagic stroke rests on case reports that the Discussion itself says may reflect reporting bias; the epidemiological support (two studies) is real but uses amphetamine-use codes in one and is given without intervals. The abstract states that the incidence of methamphetamine-related stroke "will increase" as a certainty, which is a projection, not a finding. The Discussion infers that, because many reports did not mention other risk factors, haemorrhagic strokes were related primarily to methamphetamine use, which treats unreported as absent (the authors add that unreported risk factors cannot be excluded). The outcome figures in the abstract do not say that deaths identified at autopsy were included. The Discussion calls methamphetamine likely to be making a disproportionate contribution to rising stroke incidence in young people, citing no study that measured this.

timeline.event: Kaku & Lowenstein case-control study of stroke in people aged 15–44: illicit drug use relative risk 6.5 (ischaemic) and 11.7 (haemorrhagic) at age 35 or below; 12 strokes attributed to amphetamine (Table 3)
Petitti et al. case-control study of women aged 15–44: amphetamine use associated with 3.8 times the risk of stroke (Table 3)
Westover, McBride & Haley population-based study of hospitalized stroke at ages 18–44 (Texas): OR 4.95 for haemorrhagic and 1.04 for ischaemic stroke with amphetamine use (Table 3)
Ho et al. series of 30 methamphetamine-associated strokes (20 haemorrhagic, 10 ischaemic, all ages); one autopsy showed accelerated atherosclerosis without vasculitis
Huang et al. 10-year follow-up of 1315 people who used methamphetamine: HR 2.09 for haemorrhagic stroke, no difference for ischaemic stroke (Table 3)
Darke, Lappin, Kaye & Duflou national study of 38 fatal methamphetamine-related strokes in Australia; reported by Hemphill et al. (2024) as finding no necrotizing angiitis

Hemphill et al. narrative review of methamphetamine and stroke in the young: cites this review for the over-80% haemorrhagic share and the inhalation-predominant route in ischaemic cases, describes Beadell et al. as an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage cohort, and judges vasculitis a rare mechanism to be invoked with skepticism

replication.where_it_stands: The most-cited review of methamphetamine and stroke in young adults, but its headline proportions (80% haemorrhagic; a third fatal) are properties of the published case literature, not of people who use methamphetamine. The association with haemorrhagic stroke rests on two epidemiological studies (Westover 2007; Huang 2016) that need their own cards; the absence of an association with ischaemic stroke in both deserves equal weight.

funding.funder: Not reported (no funding statement in the published article).
funding.declared_conflicts: Competing interests: none declared (Footnotes). Provenance: not commissioned; externally peer reviewed.
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors at the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, UNSW Sydney (first author also School of Psychiatry, UNSW). Shane Darke is a co-author of one of the three included post-mortem series (Kaye et al. 2008, Table 2) and of several background references. The contributors statement says the first author ran the searches and analyses; no second screener or extractor is named (an acknowledged colleague assisted with the literature review).

what_would_settle_it: A population-based cohort or a large case-control study of young adults with stroke that verifies methamphetamine exposure by toxicology, separates methamphetamine from other amphetamines, adjusts for smoking, hypertension, other stimulants and vascular malformations, and reports incidence of haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke as absolute rates with confidence intervals; for prognosis, a registry comparing outcomes of drug-associated and other strokes at the same ages, excluding cases ascertained at autopsy.

domains.domain: Item 1: research question and inclusion criteria include population, exposure, comparator and outcome
domains.note: Population (aged 44 or younger), exposure (non-medical methamphetamine or amphetamine use) and outcome (stroke) are stated; no comparator.

domains.domain: Item 2 (critical): protocol established before the review
Item 3: choice of study designs explained
domains.note: Case reports, autopsy series and epidemiological studies were all included without justification or separate weighting.
Three databases, listed terms, full strategy in a supplement, reference-list searching; English-language restriction not justified, no grey literature or expert contact.
Not described; the first author performed the searches.

domains.domain: Item 7 (critical): list of excluded studies with reasons
domains.note: Only a flow diagram (image); no list in the article.

domains.domain: Item 8: included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 1–3 give each case or study; route of administration and how drug use was established are not shown per case.

domains.domain: Item 9 (critical): satisfactory technique for assessing risk of bias in individual studies
domains.note: No appraisal of the epidemiological studies and no causality assessment of the case attributions.

domains.domain: Item 10: funding sources of included studies reported
Item 13 (critical): risk of bias accounted for when interpreting results
domains.note: Reporting bias and severity bias of the case literature are acknowledged, but confounding in the epidemiological studies is not discussed and the conclusions are not tempered.
Differences in drug-implicated proportions across hospital series are attributed to local use rates and time trends; no formal exploration.

domains.domain: Item 16: conflicts of interest and funding of the review reported
domains.note: Competing interests declared (none); no funding statement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four of the applicable critical items are not met (no protocol, no list of excluded studies, no risk-of-bias or causality assessment, risk of bias not accounted for in interpretation); items 11, 12 and 15 do not apply because there is no meta-analysis. The search is reasonable and the case table is unusually complete, which makes the review a good catalogue of published cases; but the headline proportions describe what gets published, not what happens to people who use methamphetamine.

key_findings.finding: Search of EMBASE, MEDLINE and PsycINFO to 10 February 2017 plus reference lists; 370 records screened and 77 papers included: 3 post-mortem series, 11 case-control and epidemiological studies, 63 case reports and series.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Methods, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 (image, not extracted)

key_findings.finding: Post-mortem series: intracranial haemorrhage caused 2 of 146 (1.4%; berry aneurysm with subarachnoid haemorrhage), 10 of 413 (2.4%) and 17 of 371 (5%) all-age methamphetamine-related deaths (Logan et al. 1998; Karch et al. 1999; Kaye et al. 2008). Karch et al. found no such cases in 114 drug-free trauma deaths; Kaye et al. found cerebrovascular complications significantly more common in women.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 10/413 versus 0/114 gives a two-sided Fisher exact p of about 0.13; the strong association attributed to Karch et al. is not shown by these counts alone.

key_findings.finding: Hospital series implicated amphetamines in 6–13% of haemorrhagic strokes and 2–6% of ischaemic strokes; in an Adelaide series of ischaemic stroke at ages 15–50, 19 of 326 (6%) involved amphetamines, predominantly injected, compared with 1 of 51 (2%) in a US series a decade earlier.
key_findings.note: The 6% from Kaku & Lowenstein is 12 of 214 strokes of both types, not a share of haemorrhagic strokes.

key_findings.finding: Westover et al. (population-based, hospitalized stroke at ages 18–44; 937 haemorrhagic, 998 ischaemic): amphetamine use associated with haemorrhagic stroke, OR 4.95, and not with ischaemic stroke, OR 1.04; the haemorrhagic association was more than double that for cocaine or tobacco, and amphetamine use was associated with higher mortality after haemorrhagic stroke.
key_findings.note: No confidence intervals or covariates are given in the review; the text calls the odds ratio a 4.95 increased risk. Exposure is described as amphetamine use.

key_findings.finding: Huang et al. (1315 people who used methamphetamine, all ages, 54 stroke events, 10-year follow-up): HR 2.09 (p=0.001) for haemorrhagic stroke versus a control group; no significant difference for ischaemic stroke or subarachnoid haemorrhage. Petitti et al. (women aged 15–44; 1021 controls): amphetamine use associated with 3.8 times the risk of stroke, with no separate estimate by stroke type.

Case reports: 98 strokes at ages 16–44, of which 81 haemorrhagic (83%) and 17 ischaemic. Haemorrhagic: men to women 2:1 (editors' count 51:30); route oral:injection:inhalation 3:3:1; 60 intracerebral and 32 subarachnoid haemorrhages (13 both); intraventricular haemorrhage in 5 (1 without intracerebral haemorrhage); aneurysm 17%, arteriovenous malformation 8%, other vascular abnormalities (beading, arteritis, small-artery occlusion) in a third, no vascular abnormality in 47%.
key_findings.note: Denominators for 17%, 8% and 47% are not stated. Editors' count from Table 1: 11 definite and 1 possible aneurysm (6 of them from autopsy series) and 5 arteriovenous malformations among 81 cases. Route cannot be checked: Table 1 has no route column.

key_findings.finding: Haemorrhagic stroke outcomes: death in a third, complete recovery in a quarter, residual deficits in about 40%. Editors' count from Table 1: 26 of 81 died (32%) and 19–21 recovered fully (23–26%, depending on whether 'fair' and 'almost asymptomatic' recovery are counted); excluding the 10 autopsy-series cases, 16 of 71 died (23%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Haemorrhagic stroke, 2nd paragraph; Table 1 (footnote † marks autopsy series)

key_findings.finding: Ischaemic stroke (17 cases): men to women 12:5; route oral:injection:inhalation 1:1:4; mostly anterior-circulation territory; where angiography was done, beading in 3, intimal thickening in 1, normal in 4; other causes in 3 (bacterial embolus 1, carotid dissection 2). Death about 20%, complete recovery about 20%, residual deficits about 60%.
key_findings.note: Editors' count from Table 1: 3 of 17 died, 3 of 17 recovered fully; 7 of 17 are recorded as smokers.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the 80% haemorrhagic share is far above the 40–55% expected in stroke at ages under 45 and may partly reflect reporting bias, and that the reported outcomes may reflect the severe end of the spectrum because minor events would not be reported.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Prognosis and outcomes

key_findings.finding: Proposed mechanisms are hypertension and tachycardia, vasculitis (necrotizing angiitis, beading on angiography, in some cases resolving on repeat angiography after stopping use or after corticosteroids), direct vascular toxicity, vasospasm and accelerated atherosclerosis; supporting evidence is case reports, a 2009 series of 30 cases that found no vasculitis in ischaemic stroke, and a 1971 study in rhesus monkeys given intravenous methamphetamine over 2 weeks.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Pathogenesis of haemorrhagic stroke; Pathogenesis of ischaemic stroke

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine-associated aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage had worse outcomes than age-matched controls at discharge (Beadell et al., 28 of 374 with methamphetamine) and methamphetamine use independently predicted poorer Glasgow Outcome Scale scores at 1 and 3 years (Moon et al., 31 of 398).

reporting_issues.issue: The inclusion criteria restrict cases to people aged 44 or younger, but Table 2 (three post-mortem series) and most of Table 3 (Ho, Beadell, Moon, Nakagawa, Huang; Phillips at 15–50) are all-age or older-age studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: The post-mortem and epidemiological findings do not describe young adults specifically; any claim about young people should rest on Westover et al. (18–44), Petitti et al. and Kaku & Lowenstein (15–44), or the case reports.

reporting_issues.issue: Title, abstract and conclusions refer to methamphetamine, but by the editors' count 46 of the 98 cases in Table 1 (43 of 81 haemorrhagic) involved amphetamine, dextroamphetamine or amphetamine with ecstasy without methamphetamine being named; the Westover estimate concerns amphetamine use.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should say methamphetamine or amphetamine; the proportions are not specific to methamphetamine.

reporting_issues.issue: Ischaemic case fatality is given as one-fifth in the abstract and about 20% in the Results, but as one quarter in the Discussion (Prognosis and outcomes); Table 1 shows 3 of 17 (18%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Use one-fifth (3 of 17) if cited at all.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says haemorrhagic stroke was associated with vascular abnormalities in a third of cases; the Results give aneurysm 17%, arteriovenous malformation 8%, other abnormalities a third and no abnormality 47%, implying abnormalities in about half.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract understates pre-existing or coexisting vascular lesions, which bear on whether the drug was the cause.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say intracerebral haemorrhages were predominantly temporal, parietal and occipital; in Table 1 the editors count frontal involvement in 13 cases, parietal in 15, temporal in 5 and occipital in 2 (mixed sites counted under each lobe).
reporting_issues.consequence: The anatomical distribution in the text does not match the case table; do not cite it.

reporting_issues.issue: The text cites three studies of haemorrhagic stroke (refs 32–34) as reporting methamphetamine use in 7–13% of cases; refs 33 and 34 are single case reports (one of them an ischaemic infarction), and Table 3 assigns the 7% and 8% figures to refs 30 and 31.
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation numbering error; the figures belong to Beadell et al., Moon et al. and Nakagawa et al.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 describes Beadell et al. (ref 30) as an all-age spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage cohort; the reference title and the Discussion describe aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage.
reporting_issues.consequence: The stroke type of that cohort must be checked in the primary paper before its 7% figure is used; Hemphill et al. (2024) also describe it as an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage study.

reporting_issues.issue: Background figures for the haemorrhagic share of stroke in young people differ: 33.5% at ages 20–44 in the Introduction (ref 13) versus 40–55% under 45 in the Discussion (ref 12). The outcome comparator in the Discussion (ref 67) is described as all-cause stroke at ages 16–45, but by title it is a study of ischaemic stroke in young adults.
reporting_issues.consequence: The contrast between methamphetamine-related cases and young stroke in general is drawn against inconsistent or mismatched baselines.

reporting_issues.issue: The haemorrhagic death rate pools 10 autopsy-series cases (Table 1 footnote †) with clinical cases, and one counted death (Ago et al. 2006) is attributed in Table 1 to methamphetamine poisoning with renal failure from rhabdomyolysis rather than to the stroke.
reporting_issues.consequence: Case fatality is overstated by design; excluding autopsy-series cases it falls from 32% to 23% (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: No confidence intervals are given for any odds ratio, relative risk or hazard ratio, and covariates are not reported; odds ratios are described as increased risk.
reporting_issues.consequence: Each estimate must be taken from its primary paper with its interval and adjustment set.

reporting_issues.issue: The article carries no funding statement; supplementary files (search strategy, full references for Table 1) are PDFs and were not read.
reporting_issues.consequence: Funding is recorded as not reported; individual case citations not given in the reference list could not be checked.
